method: WebSearch retrieval. Search returned summarized content, so most items are labeled paraphrase (with quoted fragments preserved where the results presented them in quotation marks). All URLs exactly as returned; nothing invented.
angle_summary: Across Finch, Routinery, Tiimo, Structured, Sunsama, Motion, Todoist, Goblin Tools, Numo, Inflow, Lunatask, Amazing Marvin, and Llama Life, ADHD users describe a repeating failure loop: apps hook them with novelty, then demand exactly the executive functions ADHD impairs (daily manual planning, setup, consistency). Streaks and overdue-task counts convert inevitable inconsistency into shame, notifications habituate into invisibility, plans stop at the list without helping execution, and pricey subscriptions plus dark-pattern cancellation flows turn the category into an 'ADHD tax.' The gap is a system designed for inconsistent engagement: near-zero setup, guilt-free re-entry after absence, novelty-preserving cues, and execution support.

problems.name: Streaks and gamified consistency trigger shame spirals and app abandonment
problems.frequency_signal: Named the single most common failure pattern in multiple ADHD-focused design analyses (Klarity, Kabit, Sprout); a whole sub-genre of 'guilt-free' apps now markets itself around not punishing missed days.

evidence.text: For people with ADHD, streak features often create anxiety, avoidance, and eventually app abandonment; when a streak breaks — practically inevitable given ADHD executive-function challenges — users report feelings of failure disproportionate to the setback, leading to complete abandonment of the app and the habit it supported.

Streak-based habit trackers called the single worst design choice for ADHD users: ADHD brains have inherently inconsistent days, and a streak system punishes that inconsistency, creating shame spirals.

Finch's flip side: because streaks never penalize missed days, accountability is softened — no streak stats, completion-rate analytics, or long-term calendar views; some anxious users still report the goal structure sending them into panic attacks.

problems.existing_solutions: Finch and Tiimo remove punishment entirely; Klarity recommends cumulative tracking, optional streak visibility, recovery mechanics.
problems.gap: No mainstream app offers accountability that survives absence: cumulative/bounce-back progress models that welcome the user back without guilt yet still give meaningful long-term metrics. Apps pick either guilt (streaks) or no feedback (Finch), not resilient feedback.

problems.name: Setup and daily-maintenance burden demands the executive function users don't have
problems.frequency_signal: Appears in reviews of nearly every 'serious' planner; Amazing Marvin shipped a workflow library specifically to reduce feature overwhelm.

evidence.text: Sunsama requires roughly 15-20 minutes of manual planning every day (80+ hours/year); if you skip the morning ritual it 'loses most of its value' — early on it feels like the app is 'constantly asking you to do one more thing before you can just start working.'

Amazing Marvin's sheer number of options overwhelms some users; the learning curve is 'a bit overwhelming' at first, particularly for folks with ADHD; the developer shipped premade workflow setups in response.
Motion complaints: difficult onboarding, cluttered UI, weak mobile app, Reddit users who found the app too complicated — despite being marketed as ADHD-friendly automation.
Many traditional planners require so much setup or maintenance that they overwhelm ADHD brains; the planner 'just becomes one more thing you are behind on.'

problems.existing_solutions: Marvin's premade workflows; Motion's AI auto-scheduling (heavy onboarding); Goblin Tools' zero-setup single-purpose tools.
problems.gap: A tool useful on day one with zero configuration AND graceful degradation — keeps functioning (auto-triaging, auto-resurfacing) during the weeks the user doesn't plan, instead of becoming stale and shame-inducing.

problems.name: Notification blindness: reminders habituate into background noise within days
problems.frequency_signal: A named phenomenon across multiple ADHD reminder guides; notification failures among top recurring complaints in Tiimo's app-store reviews.

evidence.text: 'Notification blindness': ADHD brains stop responding to single alerts, repeated identical tones get filtered like background noise within about a week, alarms trigger automatic swiping rather than action.

Tiimo user reviews report the app 'as a reminder app never sends reminder notifications,' notifications not working despite being enabled, random sign-outs — fatal flaws for people using it to externalize time.
Routinery users can't get a quiet 'ding' between steps — only text-to-speech or push; critique questions whether the timer nagging is more annoying than helpful.

problems.existing_solutions: Guides recommend multi-sensory, varied, novelty-preserving sounds and context-tied reminders; smartwatch haptics.
problems.gap: No major app systematically fights habituation — rotating modalities, escalating only for high-stakes items, context-aware timing, or detecting dismiss-without-act patterns and changing strategy.

problems.name: Capture-without-execution: task graveyards and plans that stop at the list
problems.frequency_signal: 'Task graveyard' and 'app graveyard' are recurring named concepts; industry retention data shows the pattern quantitatively.

evidence.text: Todoist 'Graveyard' failure mode: users capture everything, never review, hit 87+ overdue tasks within a month, opening the app triggers shame, and they stop opening it; Todoist is 'a storage system, not an execution system.'
Goblin Tools' Magic ToDo 'generates a beautiful list of steps and then stops at the plan' — a planning tool, not an execution tool; for many ADHD users the list was never the problem.
Survival analysis of mobile mental-health/self-care app usage found median 15-day retention of ~3.9% and median 30-day retention of ~3.3% — roughly 95%+ of day-1 users gone within a month.
Phones full of productivity apps sitting like 'digital ghosts,' abandoned after day three once novelty fades — the novelty-then-quit cycle framed as the default outcome.

problems.existing_solutions: Two-tool stacks (capture in Todoist, execute in Llama Life); Goblin Tools for breakdown; body-doubling services.
problems.gap: Nothing closes the loop from captured task → initiated action in one place: auto-decaying/archiving stale tasks so the graveyard never forms, shame-free list resets, and initiation scaffolding built into the same tool that captures.

problems.name: Subscription fatigue and the 'ADHD tax': premium pricing plus cancellation dark patterns
problems.frequency_signal: Pricing/cancellation complaints appear in reviews of at least six of thirteen apps covered.

evidence.text: Inflow reviewers report being charged despite canceling within the trial window, charged two years in a row while unable to cancel, and one reviewer alleging the maker deliberately makes canceling difficult, 'banking on users with ADHD not being able to manage multiple cancellation steps'; the $130-$200/yr price questioned.
Trustpilot/app-store feedback on Tiimo includes complaints that canceling the subscription is 'almost impossible,' alongside bug and reminder-failure reports.
Recent Routinery reviews describe an aggressive paywall — free tier cut to two routines, previously free features moved behind $7.99/mo, the app 'harassing you to subscribe.'

A Numo App Store reviewer complains the $15-16/month price is too expensive specifically for an ADHD-targeted app; ADHD-Friendly explains how ADHD turns free trials into months of paying for unused services — the 'ADHD tax.'
evidence.source: ADHD-Friendly blog + Numo App Store reviews (apps.apple.com id1628994767)

problems.existing_solutions: Free/no-paywall planner roundups; Goblin Tools' near-free pricing; bundles like Setapp.
problems.gap: An honest-pricing position is wide open: cheap pricing, trial-expiry warnings, one-tap cancellation, pause-instead-of-cancel, 'you haven't used this in 30 days — want to stop paying?' prompts. No incumbent ships anti-ADHD-tax billing; it's a trust wedge.

problems.name: Rigid schedules collide with time blindness and variable-capacity days
problems.frequency_signal: Recurs across reviews of Structured, Motion, and general ADHD planner guidance.

evidence.text: ADDA warns strict hourly layouts may not work for adults with ADHD because time blindness makes it hard for things to go as scheduled, recommending broad blocks; Structured's visual timeline 'can become stressful if you fill every part of the day with tasks.'
Motion packs the day too tightly, leaving no room for unplanned work; the algorithm 'optimizes for fitting everything in' and produces an oppressive schedule.

Mainstream productivity systems assume consistent energy, reliable working memory, a stable internal sense of time, and on-demand task initiation — assumptions that almost never hold for ADHD; when the system fails, cultural narrative blames the user, and shame worsens executive function for the next attempt.

problems.existing_solutions: Motion auto-reschedules (but re-packs just as tightly); Tiimo avoids red 'failed' states; guides recommend under-scheduling.
problems.gap: No app plans around variable capacity: energy-aware 'low-spoon day' mode that auto-shrinks the plan, deliberate slack enforcement, graceful mid-day replanning that reframes derailment as normal.
